assumptions._aumGrowthWhy: FY27 management assessment (29-Apr-2026): 22-24%; long-term corridor 23-25%. Q1FY27 grew 24% with a record ₹36,969 cr added in one quarter, MSME back to growth from Q3 and gold loans to ₹29-31k cr by Mar-27 (call, 30-Jul-2026). We take the top of FY27 guidance, then fade 1pp a year as the book passes ₹8 lakh cr; FY26 itself fell short of its 24-25% guide (22%).
assumptions._yieldOnAumWhy: Interest income ÷ average AUM: 16.4% FY25, 15.7% FY26, 15.5% annualised in Q1FY27. Management guides a 10-15bp NIM moderation in FY27; the mix keeps shifting to lower-yield gold, mortgages and loans against securities; the RBI's draft ban on revolving credit for NBFCs (6-Aug-2026) puts ~50bp of extra yield on the ~14% flexi book at risk (Jefferies). We take ~15-20bp off each year.
assumptions._feeIncomePctWhy: Non-interest income ÷ average AUM: 2.06% FY25, 1.99% FY26, 2.0% in Q1FY27. Guidance: non-interest income +16-18% in FY27 vs AUM +22-24%, so the ratio drifts down.
assumptions._costOfFundsWhy: Interest expense ÷ average Screener borrowings (incl. deposits): 7.64% FY25, 7.26% FY26 (the company's own measure: 7.97% and 7.54%). Reported cost of funds was 7.40% in Q1FY27, 14bp below FY26; management expects it 'range bound with a slight upward bias' as incremental funding is 30-60bp dearer (call, 30-Jul-2026).
assumptions._opexPctWhy: Operating expenses incl. depreciation ÷ average AUM: 3.99% FY25, 3.78% FY26. Guidance: opex to net total income 25-40bp better in FY27 despite gold-loan/MFI branch openings and the Labour Codes; AI-led productivity. These values give a cost-to-income ratio of ~32.7% in FY27E (33.0% on our FY26 basis) falling ~30bp a year.
assumptions._creditCostWhy: Provisions ÷ average AUM: 1.90% FY25, 2.05% FY26 (incl. a ₹1,406 cr accelerated ECL charge). FY27 guidance 1.45-1.60% of average AUF; Q1FY27 1.54% incl. a ₹296 cr overlay (1.31% without). 1.50% of AUM ≈ 1.53% of AUF: mid-guidance, keeping room for further overlays. FY29E edges up as a normal cycle: FY23-FY26 ranged 0.96-2.09% (company basis).
assumptions._payoutWhy: FY26 dividend ₹6.00 per share incl. a ₹0.60 special from the BHFL stake sale (19.6% of EPS); ex-special 17.7%. FY24-FY25 payout 15-16%.
assumptions._minorityPctWhy: Minority interest in Bajaj Housing Finance. FY26 ₹315 cr (1.6% of PAT) at an 86.7-88.75% stake. Management will cut the stake to 75% (public-float rule), 'first protocol' before any capital raise (call, 30-Jul-2026). We assume two tranches (H2FY27, H1FY28), BHFL profit +21%/+21%/+20% (Q1FY27 +23%, AUM +24%): minority ₹0.46k / 0.88k / 1.13k cr.
assumptions._otherIncomeWhy: Screener 'other income' outside operations: ₹19-33 cr a year before exceptional items (FY24-FY26); FY26 included a ₹284 cr Labour Code charge.
assumptions._capitalRaiseWhy: Not new shares: the parent's equity gain from selling ~11.7% of BHFL down to 75% (5.85% each in H2FY27 and H1FY28) at ₹82 (30-Sep-2026 close), less ~14.6% tax on the gain (BFL cost ~₹12.2 a share) and less the minority interest created at book. valuation._why: Ke = 6.5% + 1.1 × 6% = 13.1% (house rf and ERP; beta 1.1 for a large, rate- and credit-sensitive lender). sustainableRoe 20% = middle of the company's long-term 19-21% corridor. g = 10% long-run book growth in the justified P/B (about nominal GDP; below the 15-16% the franchise can fund today). Residual income fades ROE to 20% over 8 years, payout rising to 30%, 6% terminal growth.

methods.name: P/B
methods.why: The street's method (Motilal Oswal 4.8x FY28E, Nomura 4.2x Sep-28E, ICICI Direct 4.4x FY28E standalone + subsidiaries). 4.0x = own median forward P/B since Apr-2021 (4.6x) × the listed-lender move vs five-year medians (−4.5%) × the growth regime since Apr-2023 (4.2x ÷ 4.6x). Bull 4.6x = median since 2021; bear 3.4x = lowest since 2021.

methods.name: Justified P/B
methods.why: (ROE − g) ÷ (Ke − g) = (20 − 10) ÷ (13.1 − 10) on book at the 12-month target date.

methods.name: Residual income
methods.why: Book plus the present value of profit above the 13.1% cost of equity, ROE fading to 20%, rolled forward 6 months.

methods.name: P/E
methods.why: Cross-check only. 20x = median forward P/E since Apr-2021 (25.7x, no trough years) × listed-lender P/E move vs five-year medians (−13.6%) × growth regime since Apr-2023 (23.2x ÷ 25.7x). Bull = median; bear = lowest since 2021.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Guidance raised after Q2: AUM +26/25/24% (Nomura-style 25%+), the revolving-credit draft softened (yield +10bp), credit cost stays near Q1's 1.31% (−20bp), AI keeps opex 5bp lower; long-run ROE 22%.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: Revolving credit banned as drafted and flexi customers lost (AUM +19/18/17%, yield −30bp), funding 20bp dearer, credit cost back at ~2.1% (FY26 level incl. one-offs); long-run ROE 17%.

cover.headline: The credit cycle has turned for India's largest consumer lender and the stock sits below its usual multiple; the catch is that the price already assumes ~20% returns for ever
cover.lead: Bajaj Finance lends to 124 million Indians across consumer durables, personal, gold, small-business and home loans, and has compounded profit ~31% a year for a decade at an average return on equity of ~20%. After two costly years for credit (loan losses 2.1% of loans in FY26, incl. a ₹1,406 cr one-off charge), Q1FY27 showed the turn: losses 1.31% before a ₹296 cr precautionary overlay, profit +28%, ROE 20.4%. The street values the stock on **P/B (4.2-4.8x FY28E or Sep-28E book)**. We forecast EPS of ₹41.0 / ₹48.5 / ₹57.4 for FY27-29E and ROE of ~20%. Applying **4x to Sep-28E book of ₹286** (derived from its own 4.6x median since 2021, the sector's move and slower growth) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with BUY.** Be clear about the risk: our intrinsic cross-checks (justified P/B ₹779, residual income ₹879) sit below the price, which already implies a ~{{dcf.impliedRoe|pct0}} ROE for ever. Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.h: Credit costs are coming down, and that drives FY27
arguments.p: Loan losses were 2.09% of average loans in FY26 (1.93% before one-offs) and 1.54% in Q1FY27 including a ₹296 cr overlay; Stage 2 and 3 loans fell to 1.87%, and new-loan vintages are "below FY'20, our pre-COVID benchmark" (MD). Guidance is 1.45-1.60% for FY27. At 1.50% of AUM, profit grows {{F.patGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27E (~26% on FY26 profit before one-offs).

arguments.h: A franchise few lenders can copy
arguments.p: 124 million customers, 5.1 million added in Q1 alone, 63% of business from existing customers, 2.5 lakh points of sale, a ₹68,500 cr deposit book and AAA ratings. Opex is 33% of income even after funding gold-loan and microfinance branch roll-outs. Gold loans (+112%), consumer finance (+38-49%) and mortgages (+27%) carry growth while small-business loans are pruned.

arguments.h: But margins are slipping and the regulator is circling
arguments.p: NIM falls from {{fin.nim.11|pct}} in FY26 to {{F.nim.2|pct}} by FY29E in our model as the mix shifts to cheaper secured loans. The RBI's draft rule of 6-Aug-2026 would bar NBFCs from revolving credit; brokers put Bajaj's flexi loans at ~13-15% of AUM. This is the third RBI action touching its consumer book since Nov-2023, and a fresh equity raise was put to the board on 24-Sep-2026.

arguments.h: Valuation: below its history, not cheap on fundamentals
arguments.p: At ₹959 the stock trades at 3.6x our FY28E book and 19.8x FY28E EPS, against a 4.6x median forward P/B since 2021. Our 4x Sep-28E book gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}. A ₹15,000 cr raise at today's price would lift book per share ~6% (target ~₹1,220 at the same multiple) but cut ROE by ~1.3pp, so we treat it as roughly neutral.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): management promised to revisit FY27 guidance (AUM growth, credit cost, overlays) after one more quarter.
The equity raise: the board meets at the start of October to consider a QIP and/or a preferential issue; size and price will set the dilution.
RBI's final rules on revolving credit for NBFCs (draft of 6-Aug-2026): how much of the ~13-15% flexi book has to be re-papered, and at what yield.
Sell-down of Bajaj Housing Finance from 86.7% to 75%, which management called the "first protocol" for capital.
Succession: a decision on Rajeev Jain's renewal (term ends Mar-2028) is due by December 2027-January 2028.

sections.title: A diversified consumer and small-business lender with a deposit licence and 124 million customers

blocks.p: Bajaj Finance (BFL) is India's largest non-bank lender (NBFC). It describes itself as "a diversified non-bank with a deposit taking license", focused on "mass and affluent" customers. It earns money the way every lender does: it borrows at ~7.4% (Q1FY27 cost of funds), lends at ~15-16% on average, and keeps the gap after operating costs (~3.8% of loans) and loan losses (~1.5-2%). In FY26 interest was ₹72,776 cr of its ₹81,990 cr income and fees and other income ₹9,214 cr (insurance distribution, fees on loans and cards, payments).

The group has three lending arms. **Bajaj Finance** itself (AUM ₹4.00 lakh cr in Jun-2026) runs consumer, personal, small-business, gold, microfinance, vehicle and commercial loans. **Bajaj Housing Finance** (BHFL, listed, 86.7% owned, AUM ₹1.50 lakh cr) does home loans, loans against property, lease-rental discounting and developer finance. **Bajaj Financial Securities** (100%) does broking and margin-trade finance (₹9,770 cr). Bajaj Finserv, the group holding company, owns 51.3% of BFL; the promoter group 54.7%.

blocks.callout: **Why this matters:** Bajaj Finance is not one business but ten, each priced for its own risk: from loans against shares and gold (near-zero losses) to unsecured personal and small-business loans (where most of the losses sit). The group can shift growth between them, which is exactly what it did in FY26 (pruning MSME, pushing gold and consumer finance). The cost is that the blended yield falls as safer books grow.

sections.title: Two decades of compounding, punctuated by Covid, the regulator and capital raises

blocks.p: AUM compounded 34% a year from FY08 to FY26 (company snapshot). The record shows a pattern: growth outruns retained profit, so equity is topped up every few years; the regulator steps in when processes lag growth (2023); and credit costs spike in bad years (FY20-21, FY25-26) but have never wiped out profit.

sections.title: Retail lending in India: big runway, crowded field, and a regulator that has tightened three times in three years

blocks.p: India's retail credit runway is long but no longer empty. Bajaj Finance's MD put consumer debt at about 41% of GDP, a ratio that rose ~2pp a year for four years and ~1pp last year (Q1FY27 call). He also said bureau data now show unsecured delinquencies flat to better year on year, after the stress of FY25-26 in small-business, personal and microfinance loans that pushed Bajaj's own loan losses to ~2% and made it prune MSME lending from Jul-2025. Competition comes from every side: in Jain's words, "PSU banks, private banks, nonbanks, all three competing", plus fintech platforms in personal loans (Nomura, Aug-2026).

Among listed retail NBFCs, Bajaj Finance is the largest by far (market value ₹5.97 lakh cr on 30-Sep-2026, ~2.6x the next, Shriram Finance) and among the most profitable. On FY26 numbers hit by one-off charges its ROE (18.4%) trailed only Muthoot Finance (gold loans) and Cholamandalam, and its return on assets was second only to Muthoot's; vehicle and diversified lenders (Shriram, L&T Finance, M&M Financial, Aditya Birla Capital) earn 11-16%.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the market is big enough for Bajaj Finance to keep growing 20%+ for years. The constraints are not demand but **regulation** (each rule change has landed hardest on the largest, most digital consumer lender), **capital** (125% risk weights and ~5x leverage limits mean growth needs equity) and **price competition** from banks in the safest segments (home loans, loans against property), where Bajaj earns less.

blocks.p: An industry trend only matters to a shareholder if the company turns it into profit. We score each one.

verdicts: Q1FY27 loan losses 1.31% before the overlay vs 1.93% in FY26 before one-offs; Stage 2+3 down to 1.87%; bureau data improving in personal, business and professional loans (call).
The single biggest driver of FY27 profit growth in our model.
Urban and rural consumer finance +38% and +49% in Q1, but management says about half of that is higher product prices (phones, appliances), not more customers.

Profitable and low-risk, but tied to a commodity price.

BHFL AUM +24%, pristine asset quality (GNPA 0.29%), but ROE only 12.5%.
Adds size but dilutes group ROE; BFL is selling down to 75%.
Revolving-credit draft, 125% risk weights, product-level actions.

blocks.source: Q1FY27 presentation and call; Nomura (21-Aug-2026); GAM Research

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the trend that matters most in FY27 (lower credit costs) is cyclical, not structural. The structural tailwinds (AI efficiency, cross-sell to a 124 million customer base) are real but worth tens of basis points a year, while the structural headwinds (regulation, mix shift to secured loans, competition) cost about the same. That is why we model ROE flat at ~20%, not rising.

sections.title: Growth comes from mining 124 million customers, and the mix is tilting to safer loans

blocks.p: The engine is the customer base. Bajaj Finance added 17.5 million customers in FY26 and 5.1 million in Q1FY27, to 124.4 million; 79.2 million of them (64%) qualify for cross-sell offers. It booked 52.5 million loans in FY26 and expects 60-62 million in FY27; guidance for new customers was raised from 15-17 million to 18-20 million in Q1. Existing customers bring 63% of business, which lowers acquisition cost and credit risk because the company already knows their repayment history.

blocks.p: Net interest margin (NII ÷ average AUM, our basis) peaked at {{fin.nim.8|pct}} in FY23 and was {{fin.nim.11|pct}} in FY26. The yield on AUM fell from {{fin.yieldOnAum.9|pct}} (FY24) to {{fin.yieldOnAum.11|pct}} as the mix moved to mortgages, gold and loans against securities. The cost of funds peaked at 7.97% in FY25 (company basis) and fell to 7.54% in FY26 and 7.40% in Q1FY27, which cushioned the fall. That cushion is now gone: management says incremental funding is 30-60bp dearer and expects the cost of funds to stay "range bound with a slight upward bias".

blocks.p: **The revolving-credit risk, in numbers.** The RBI's draft of 6-Aug-2026 would let NBFCs offer only term loans. Brokers estimate Bajaj Finance's flexi (revolving) loans at ~13-15% of AUM, earning ~50bp more than plain term loans (Jefferies). Re-papering them as term loans at a normal yield would cost ~7bp of group yield, about 1-1.5% of profit, before any loss of customers who valued the flexibility. The larger risk is growth: flexi products sit inside the personal-loan and small-business books that already grow slowest. We cut yield by ~15-20bp a year in our base case; the bear case takes another 30bp.

blocks.p: Loan losses rose from 0.96% of average assets under finance (AUF) in FY23 to 1.93% in FY25 and 2.09% in FY26 (company basis), as stress in small-business, personal and captive two-wheeler loans hit. sections.title: Funding: AAA, diversified, and longer than its loans; a deposit book of ₹68,500 cr

blocks.p: Bajaj Finance funds itself like a high-grade corporate, not like a bank. In Jun-2026 group borrowings were 50% money markets (bonds and commercial paper), 30% bank loans, 15% public and corporate deposits (₹68,534 cr) and 5% foreign borrowings (ECB). It is rated AAA/Stable by CRISIL, ICRA, CARE and India Ratings, BBB by S&P and Baa3 by Moody's (both at India's sovereign level). The deposit licence is rare among NBFCs; deposits are 20% of Bajaj Finance's own borrowings. What it lacks is a bank's low-cost current and savings accounts, which is why its cost of funds (7.40% in Q1FY27) is well above a large bank's.

sections.title: Capital: growth needs equity every few years, and the next raise was announced on 24-Sep-2026

blocks.p: Capital adequacy (standalone) was 20.9% in Jun-2026 (Tier 1 20.01%) against a 15% minimum; group assets were 4.9x net worth (company's leverage measure; ~4.3x standalone). The constraint is not the regulatory minimum but the company's own comfort level and the 125% risk weight on consumer loans. At 22-25% AUM growth and an 18% payout, retained profit grows equity by only ~16-17% a year, so leverage creeps up. Without new equity our model takes assets to {{fin.assetsToEquity.14|n2}}x equity by FY29E, from {{fin.assetsToEquity.11|n2}}x in FY26.

On 30-Jul-2026 the MD said: "First protocol most likely will be BHFL dilution. And then if our growth momentum continues to accelerate, then ... think about capital raise", and "we don't foresee raising capital". Eight weeks later, on 24-Sep-2026, the company told the exchanges its board would meet at the start of October to consider raising equity by a QIP and/or a preferential issue. No size was given; Jefferies estimated ~₹15,000 cr (~10% of FY28E net worth) and linked it to the staggered BHFL sell-down and the Mar-2028 succession. The stock fell ~5% that day.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the raise is the price of the growth the market wants. Bajaj Finance raised equity in FY18, FY20 and FY24 and kept compounding after each; the dilution is small (~2-3% of shares) and done at 4-5x book. What grates is the message: management ruled it out on 30 July and called it eight weeks later. The company gave no reason; the RBI's August draft and the points Jefferies raised (slow BHFL sell-down, the Mar-2028 succession) are the obvious candidates, and none of them is reassuring. sections.title: From ROA to ROE: 4.5% on assets, levered ~4.5x, gives ~20%

blocks.p: A lender's return on equity is its return on assets times leverage. Bajaj Finance earns more per rupee of loans than almost any Indian lender because its yields are high and its costs and losses are controlled; it needs only ~4.5x leverage (a large bank runs at 10x+) to reach a ~20% ROE. After that, margins fall faster than costs, so ROA drifts down to {{F.roaAum.2|pct}} and ROE stays ~20% only because leverage rises. That is the honest shape of the story: a franchise holding returns by running harder, not one whose returns are expanding.

sections.title: Ten years of 30%+ profit growth, slowing to the low 20s

blocks.p: Bajaj Finance grew net profit from ₹1,279 cr in FY16 to ₹19,332 cr in FY26, about 31% a year, and book value per share about 30% a year. Only Covid broke the run: profit fell 16% in FY21 as loan losses jumped to 4% of loans. The pace has slowed since FY24. Profit grew 26% in FY24, 16% in FY25 and 15% in FY26, held back first by rising losses in unsecured consumer and small-business loans and then, in FY26, by ₹1,813 cr of one-off charges (an accelerated ₹1,406 cr provision, a ₹265 cr Labour Code charge and a ₹142 cr overlay). Before them FY26 profit grew 24%.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the machine still compounds, but at a lower gear. AUM growth has come down from 30%+ (FY19, FY24) to 22-26%, margins are slipping as the mix moves to cheaper secured loans, and the next leg of profit growth in FY27 comes largely from lower credit costs after two expensive years. We forecast EPS growth of {{F.epsGrowth.0|pct}} in FY27E (about 25% on FY26 profit before one-offs) and ~18% a year after that.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: real in data, distribution and underwriting; absent in funding

blocks.p: A lender's moat shows up as a lasting gap between what it earns on loans and what it pays for funds, costs and losses. Bajaj Finance's ROA (4-5% on AUF for a decade, except Covid) is about double that of most Indian NBFCs and banks. We test where that edge comes from and whether it is durable.

verdicts: 124 million customers, 79 million pre-qualified for cross-sell, 63% of business from existing customers; 97.7 million EMI cards in force.
Cheaper acquisition and better risk selection than any NBFC; banks have larger bases but use them less intensively.
~2.5 lakh active points of sale, 1.27 lakh consumer-durable stores; first lender most shoppers meet for EMI finance.

Cost-to-income ~33% while running 10 businesses; AI bots already originate ₹2,500 cr a quarter.

Banks win on price in secured loans (home, LAP); Bajaj must earn its spread in riskier loans.

But the moat sits in the riskier half of retail credit, it is exposed to regulation in a way a bank's is not, and it does not extend to funding. It protects returns of ~20%, not returns that rise.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean books, but provisions and presentation give management levers

blocks.p: We rate accounting **AMBER**. Joint auditors Price Waterhouse and Kirtane & Pandit gave an unmodified opinion on FY26, nothing we found suggests misstatement, and disclosure is among the best of any Indian lender (19-year history, stage-wise provisions by business, vintage curves). But four things deserve a reader's attention:

bullets: **Discretionary provisions.** ₹2,203 cr of overlays and accelerated provisions since Q4FY25 (₹359 cr, ₹1,406 cr, ₹142 cr, ₹296 cr). They are prudent, but they move profit between quarters at management's choice: Q3FY26 profit fell year on year because of them, and Q1FY27 would have been ~4% higher without one. Releases in a later year would flatter reported growth.

**Presentation change (Q4FY26).** Recoveries of written-off loans (~₹800 cr in FY26) moved from income to loan losses for all periods. Profit is unchanged, but credit cost and cost-to-income now read lower and higher respectively than before, so old and new ratios are not comparable. Screener's history mixes the two bases (FY24 and earlier old, FY25-26 new); we show both where it matters.

**Gains on selling subsidiary shares go to equity, not profit.** Selling BHFL shares adds to consolidated book value (≈₹4,300 cr in FY25 and ≈₹1,300 cr in FY26 by our reconciliation of equity) but never shows in consolidated profit; the standalone accounts book it as an exceptional gain (₹2,544 cr FY25, ₹1,166 cr FY26), which also funded a ₹0.60 special dividend.
**One-offs in both directions.** FY25 had a ₹348 cr tax benefit from court orders; FY26 a ₹265 cr Labour Code charge. Small (1-2% of profit), but reported growth in each year is distorted.

sections.title: Management and governance: a strong group, a stellar operator, and an unresolved succession

blocks.p: Rajeev Jain has led Bajaj Finance (MD from 2015) and is the architect of its model. That is below the stock's 4.6x median since 2021, which is why the street's method gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}) and a BUY. exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Non-banking financial company: a lender regulated by the RBI that cannot take current or savings deposits. "Upper layer" NBFCs (the largest) face bank-like rules.
Assets under management: all loans the group manages (incl. any sold or securitised). Assets under finance: loans on the balance sheet. AUF is ~2% below AUM.
Net interest income = interest earned − interest paid. Net interest margin = NII ÷ average AUM (our basis).
NII plus fees and other operating income: the lender's "revenue" after funding costs.
Operating expenses ÷ net total income ("opex to NTI").
Loan losses and provisions ÷ average AUM (our basis) or average AUF (company basis).
Ind AS 109 buckets: performing, under-performing (30-90 days overdue) and non-performing (90+ days) loans. ECL = expected credit loss provisions held against them.
Gross / net non-performing assets (Stage 3) as % of loans; provision coverage ratio = provisions on Stage 3 ÷ Stage 3 loans.
An extra provision booked on management's judgement (e.g. for macro risks), on top of the model-based ECL.
Capital ÷ risk-weighted assets (regulatory minimum 15% for NBFCs); Tier 1 is the core equity part.
The share of a loan counted as "risky" for capital: 125% for unsecured consumer loans since Nov-2023.
Profit ÷ average assets; profit ÷ average shareholders' equity (attributable to Bajaj Finance shareholders).
Price ÷ book value per share. Justified P/B = (ROE − g) ÷ (cost of equity − g): the multiple a steady ROE and growth rate support.
Book value plus the present value of future profit above the cost of equity.
Half FY28E plus half FY29E: the book value (or EPS) the market will look at in September 2027.
A credit line the borrower can draw, repay and redraw (like a card limit), as opposed to a term loan with a fixed schedule.
Loans against securities / margin trade finance; lease rental discounting (loans against office rents); loan against property.
Qualified institutions placement (new shares sold to institutions) / new shares sold to named buyers such as the promoter.
Bajaj Housing Finance (listed subsidiary); minimum public shareholding, the rule that pushes BFL's stake down to 75%.
